title: Putting Three ADSA Equity Goals into Practice
before: Explore how DSD supervisors and managers select three ADSA equity goals and connect them with real conditions, responsibilities, and evidence.

turns.text: This discussion introduces Putting Three ADSA Equity Goals into Practice. It’s mainly for supervisors and managers developing their three-goal work plans, and for staff who want to see how those goals connect with service delivery and workplace opportunity. The course begins with the shared understanding that the work rests on.

In the One DSD arrangement, the Equity Director briefs leadership on the six ADSA goals and answers their questions. Supervisors and managers then use the work plan to select three goals and put them into practice, with the consultant providing consultation and guidance as needed. So the course isn’t introducing a new process. It’s supporting one already in place.

The six goals, in the program’s wording, are eliminating disparities; community engagement; hiring and retention; learning and development; contracts and procurement; and communication and accessibility. You select three that are relevant to your work, with reasons. Choosing three doesn’t mean the others are unimportant, or that every course needs to address all six.

The worked example starts with a practice question: people can read a service notice but can’t use the follow-up route. The selected goals are communication and accessibility, community engagement, and contracts and procurement. The plan examines the route, the accounts of people affected, and relevant provider expectations, while actual authority and a better result remain open.

I like that the course starts by finding work that already exists. A service review, learning arrangement, or workforce practice may already address part of a goal, and a missing work-plan row doesn’t mean equity work is absent. Then it asks you to describe the condition and a possible mechanism: how a routine may repeatedly shape access, opportunity, or burden.

And then explain why the three belong together. What does each goal contribute, and where might they reinforce or complicate one another? More activity doesn’t automatically mean more progress, and a change that supports one goal may create a burden relevant to another. Community knowledge helps here, as long as it arrives while choices are still open.

There’s a workforce example too. A practice area selects hiring and retention, learning and development, and eliminating disparities, and only staff already familiar with the manager receive preparation for development assignments. You’ll consider what that plan should examine. The course traces conditions like that across recruitment, onboarding, support, development, recognition, and transition.

Responsibility needs to be understandable. A plan describes the proposed action and the actual role that can consider or carry it out. It doesn’t assign new authority, workloads, or partner duties from a template. Required policy, employment, service, and other processes continue through their responsible roles, and an accommodation, complaint, or safety issue still follows its own process.

The course also separates action from intended result. A revised notice or a supported learning opportunity is an output. Usable clarification or opportunity is the result you examine. You’ll practice with a progress update that claims community agreement and eliminated disparities from a route nobody has used yet, and decide what account the evidence supports.

Then you’ll draft your own three-goal connection. Choose a practice or actual question, explain why three goals fit, and for each name the condition, a possible action, and an evidence question. You’ll note where consultant guidance or another responsibility is needed. The course doesn’t prescribe a timetable or reporting cycle; the account can fit an existing work plan.

As you go, keep a real condition from your area in mind, something people encounter in a service or in the workplace that you’d like to understand better. Which three goals might connect to it, and why? Bring that question with you. The practice will help you shape a plan that links action, evidence, and the people who carry out the work.

guidance.title: When goals pull in different directions
guidance.text: Selected goals can support one another, but they can also compete for the same time, staff, or attention. A faster communication route may reduce one burden while shifting work to a partner or another team. Naming those tensions early helps you compare options honestly and decide where consultation would help, before an action is underway and harder to adjust.

guidance.title: Describing progress honestly
guidance.text: Think about an action already taken in your area that connects to an equity goal. What can you say with confidence about what was prepared or carried out? What remains unknown about its use or effects? Consider how you would describe a narrower gain as meaningful while leaving broader results open until there is evidence to support them.
